approach: Find acceleration as the slope of each straight segment of the v-t graph, then build the s-t graph by adding the signed area under v-t to the starting position.

steps.text: Find acceleration on each segment as the slope of the v-t line.
Start the position at s = 20 m at t = 0 and add the area under v-t up to each breakpoint.
Between breakpoints the s-t graph is straight while v is constant, and curved while v is changing linearly.
steps.equation: straight falling line for 0≤t≤4 s; curved between 4 and 12 s with a minimum s = −120 m at t = 10 s (where v = 0); curved between 12 and 14 s
steps.why_this_step: The minimum of the s-t graph occurs exactly where the velocity crosses zero.

final_answer.value: a-t graph: a = 0 from t = 0–4 s, a = 10 m/s² from t = 4–6 s, a = −10 m/s² from t = 6–8 s, a = 10 m/s² from t = 8–12 s, a = −10 m/s² from t = 12–14 s (a step graph). s-t graph passes through (0,20), (4,−60), (6,−80), (8,−100), (10,−120) [minimum, since v = 0 here], (12,−100), (14,−80) m — a straight falling line from t = 0–4 s, and curves elsewhere.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the particle keeps moving in the same direction throughout, instead of recognising the minimum position occurs at t = 10 s where the velocity is zero.
Drawing the s-t segment from t = 0 s to t = 4 s as a curve, when the velocity is constant there and the position actually falls in a straight line.
